sentence: Testicular cancer is a cancer that starts in a testicle, one of the two glands in the scrotum.
note: Plain textbook definition.

sentence: Some people with testicular cancer have no symptoms, and the most common sign is a lump or swelling in a testicle.
note: MedlinePlus: some people have none, a lump is often the first sign; CRUK/NHS list lump or swelling first.

sentence: It can affect anyone who has testicles, including trans women, and Macmillan says it is most likely between the ages of 25 and 40.
note: Macmillan: can affect anyone who has testicles, including men, trans women and people assigned male at birth; most likely between 25 and 40. 'Non-binary people' not stated in retrieved text, removed.

sentence: Most lumps in the scrotum are not cancer, and testicular cancer is rare.
note: Search summaries of NHS trust and CRUK pages: most testicular lumps are not cancer, testicular cancer is rare (page attribution blended).

sentence: MedlinePlus calls it one of the most treatable and curable cancers, and removing the affected testicle is the main treatment, according to the NHS.
note: MedlinePlus: one of the most treatable and curable cancers; NHS: main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle.

sentence: The exact cause of testicular cancer is not known, according to MedlinePlus and Macmillan
note: MedlinePlus: exact cause poorly understood; Macmillan: cause not yet understood. Original CRUK attribution not re-retrievable.

sentence: Most testicular cancers are germ cell tumours of two main types, seminoma and non-seminoma
note: PMC editorial: seminomas and non-seminomas make up most testicular cancers; Orchid/HDFT describe both as germ cell tumours. 'Cells that make sperm' dropped (not retrieved).

sentence: An undescended testicle
note: Macmillan and PMC editorial: undescended testis is the most common risk factor.

sentence: A family history of testicular cancer
note: Macmillan, MedlinePlus and PMC editorial list family history.

sentence: A previous testicular cancer
note: PMC editorial/review: prior testicular cancer; MedlinePlus: prior diagnosis.

sentence: Male infertility
note: PMC10383207 review: meta-analysis found increased risk in infertile men. Not a Macmillan/NHS listed factor.

sentence: Ethnicity, as it is more common in white men
note: Macmillan lists ethnicity; a risk-factor review says incidence is highest in white men.

sentence: A lump or swelling in a testicle, or a testicle that has become larger
note: NHS symptoms page lists these.

sentence: A scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard
note: NHS symptoms page lists this.

sentence: Tender or swollen breasts, occasionally
note: CRUK: occasionally tender or swollen breasts because of hormones; MedlinePlus lists enlarged breast tissue.

sentence: Spread to other parts of the body, such as the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, back or brain
note: MedlinePlus: symptoms may occur in lungs, abdomen, pelvis, back or brain if cancer has spread.

sentence: Effects on fertility from chemotherapy or radiotherapy
note: CRUK/Orchid: chemotherapy and radiotherapy may affect sperm production; NCI: chemotherapy can cause infertility. Lymph node surgery not retrieved, removed.

sentence: Lower testosterone levels in some people after treatment
note: PMC reviews: testosterone deficiency is a recognised late effect of testicular cancer treatment; rate varies.

sentence: A GP examines the testicles.
note: Search: the GP will examine you; lymph node check not retrieved, removed.

sentence: If cancer is possible, an urgent referral to hospital may follow, and having symptoms does not definitely mean cancer.
note: Leeds Teaching Hospitals: GP can refer urgently; NHS symptoms page: symptoms do not definitely mean cancer.

sentence: An ultrasound scan of the scrotum is the usual first test, and blood tests for substances called tumour markers are also used.
note: NCI: ultrasound first test; NHS England guideline and NCI: blood tests for AFP, beta-hCG, LDH.

sentence: The diagnosis is usually confirmed by removing the affected testicle and having a pathologist examine the tissue.
note: NHS England guideline: diagnosis confirmed by inguinal orchidectomy then pathology; biopsy only occasionally substitutes.

sentence: Macmillan and Cancer Research UK describe treatment as surgery, chemotherapy and in some cases radiotherapy, depending on the type of tumour and whether it has spread.
note: Macmillan treatment page and CRUK treatment-decisions page, per search summary (blended).

sentence: The NHS says the main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle, called orchidectomy.
note: NHS overview: main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle.

sentence: Because some treatments can affect fertility, the NHS says people are offered the chance to store sperm, known as sperm banking, before treatment starts.
note: NHS overview: offered sperm banking before treatment. Earlier 'other than removal of the testicle' was contradicted by Orchid (banking may be advised before orchidectomy).

sentence: MedlinePlus says the exact cause of testicular cancer is poorly understood.
note: MedlinePlus: exact cause poorly understood. Earlier 'no sure way to prevent' was an inference from absence and removed.

sentence: Several NHS trusts suggest checking the testicles about once a month so that a change is noticed, though MedlinePlus says experts do not know whether self-exams lower the chance of dying from testicular cancer in people without symptoms or risk factors.
note: Christie NHS FT, Essex ICB: monthly checks; MedlinePlus: not known whether self-exam lowers death risk without risk factors/symptoms (page attribution within MedlinePlus blended).

sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or a testicle that is getting bigger.
note: NHS symptoms page.

sentence: A GP appointment is the usual route, and the GP can arrange an urgent hospital referral if cancer is possible.
note: NHS: get symptoms checked by a GP; Leeds: GP can refer urgently. 'Routine' and sexual health clinic route removed (not retrieved).

sentence: Most lumps turn out to have other causes, but any new lump, swelling or unusual pain is worth having assessed.
note: Essex ICB: any new lump, swelling or unusual pain should be assessed by a GP though most are not cancer.

sentence: MedlinePlus says some people with testicular cancer have no symptoms, and that some cases do not cause symptoms until the cancer is advanced.
note: MedlinePlus: some people have none; some cases not symptomatic until advanced.

sentence: The NHS lists a lump or swelling in a testicle, a testicle getting bigger, an ache or pain in a testicle or the scrotum, and a scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard.
note: NHS symptoms page.

sentence: Cancer Research UK says a lump can be about the size of a pea or larger.
note: CRUK symptoms: size of a pea or larger. 'Small and firm' lump description not retrieved.

sentence: Less common symptoms listed by the NHS include an ache in the back or lower tummy, losing weight without trying, a cough, difficulty breathing or swallowing, and a sore or swollen chest.
note: NHS testicular cancer page lists these.

sentence: MedlinePlus adds that enlarged breast tissue can be a sign, although it can occur normally in teenage boys.
note: MedlinePlus: gynecomastia may occur but also occurs normally in adolescent boys.

sentence: When the cancer has spread, MedlinePlus says symptoms can appear in the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, back or brain.
note: MedlinePlus.

sentence: Lumps in the scrotum have many different causes, and testicular cancer is a rare cause.
note: NHS trust/CRUK summaries: most scrotal lumps are not cancer; testicular cancer is rare (blended).

sentence: Having these symptoms does not definitely mean a person has testicular cancer, the NHS says, but it is important to have them checked by a GP.
note: NHS: having them does not definitely mean you have testicular cancer; important to get them checked by a GP.

sentence: MedlinePlus and Macmillan say the exact cause of testicular cancer is not known.
note: MedlinePlus: poorly understood; Macmillan: not yet understood.

sentence: Macmillan lists an undescended testicle and a family history of the disease among the things that may raise the risk.
note: Macmillan causes page: undescended testicle, family history, ethnicity.

sentence: Macmillan also lists ethnicity, and a published review links male infertility with a higher risk of testicular cancer.
note: Macmillan lists ethnicity; PMC10383207 review: increased risk in infertile men.

sentence: Having a risk factor does not mean a person will develop the disease, and lacking one does not rule it out, Macmillan says.
note: Macmillan: having a risk factor doesn't guarantee disease, lacking one doesn't rule it out.

sentence: The NHS says testicular cancer is most common in men aged 15 to 49, while Macmillan says it is most likely between the ages of 25 and 40.
note: NHS overview: most common 15 to 49; Macmillan: most likely 25 to 40.

sentence: Macmillan and an NHS trust say non-seminomas most often affect people aged 15 to 35.
note: Macmillan and Harrogate NHS: non-seminomas most often 15 to 35.

sentence: Orchid and Cambridge University Hospitals describe seminomas as affecting people from about 25 to 55, though sources vary on the exact range.
note: Orchid and CUH: seminomas 25 to 55; other sources give 15 to 50/55 (summary).

sentence: The two main types, seminoma and non-seminoma, are both germ cell tumours, and a mix of the two can occur.
note: PMC editorial, Orchid, Harrogate NHS: both germ cell tumours; non-seminomas can be mixed.

sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or if a testicle is getting bigger.
note: NHS symptoms page.

sentence: Several NHS bodies, such as the Christie NHS Foundation Trust, suggest getting to know how the testicles normally feel, with a check about once a month, so that a new lump is noticed.
note: Christie: check monthly, roll each testicle between finger and thumb; Essex ICB similar.

sentence: The Christie says a normal testicle feels smooth and firm, and that it is normal for one testicle to be slightly larger or to hang lower.
note: Christie NHS FT page (search summary).

sentence: The epididymis, a soft coiled tube at the back of each testicle, is not a problem, and harmless cysts can form there.
note: Christie NHS FT page (search summary).

sentence: Macmillan says it is still important to have any change checked.
note: Macmillan how-to-check/main page.

sentence: Macmillan notes that a trans woman who has testicles may feel uncomfortable or upset about checking this part of the body, but that changes should still be checked.
note: Macmillan (search summary).

sentence: The GP examines the testicles.
note: Search summary: the GP will examine you.

sentence: If cancer is possible, an urgent referral to hospital may follow, and the NHS stresses that symptoms do not definitely mean cancer.
note: Leeds: urgent referral; NHS symptoms page.

sentence: The National Cancer Institute lists a testicular ultrasound, which uses sound waves to look at the testicles, as the first test.
note: NCI diagnosis page.

sentence: Blood tests for substances called tumour markers, such as AFP and beta-hCG, are also used.
note: NCI/NHS England guideline: AFP, beta-hCG and LDH are standard blood tests.

sentence: An NHS England guideline says blood for these markers is best taken before surgery when an ultrasound shows a cancer.
note: NHS England Mids and East guideline.

sentence: The diagnosis is confirmed by removing the testicle through a cut in the groin, and a pathologist then examines the tissue to identify the type of tumour.
note: NHS England guideline: inguinal orchidectomy; pathologist identifies type. Original 'sample of tissue' wording was imprecise.

sentence: The two main types of testicular cancer, seminoma and non-seminoma, are treated differently, so identifying the type is part of the diagnosis.
note: Search summary of CRUK/Macmillan/CUH treatment pages: options differ by type; pathologist identifies type.

sentence: The treatment plan also depends on whether the cancer has spread.
note: CRUK/NHS: treatment depends on type and spread.

sentence: After diagnosis, CT scans of the chest, abdomen and pelvis are commonly used to stage the cancer, together with the blood tumour markers.
note: Search summary of staging (Macmillan leaflet / NCI PDQ); exact page for each element not separable.

sentence: Macmillan and Cancer Research UK describe treatment as surgery, chemotherapy and in some cases radiotherapy, depending on the type of tumour and whether it has spread.
note: Macmillan treatment and CRUK treatment-decisions pages (blended).

sentence: The NHS says the main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle, called orchidectomy.
note: NHS overview.

sentence: Cancer Research UK says having one testicle removed does not usually affect the ability to have children, although the remaining testicle sometimes does not work as well, which could reduce fertility.
note: CRUK fertility page.

sentence: MedlinePlus says chemotherapy has greatly improved survival for people with both seminomas and non-seminomas.
note: MedlinePlus.

sentence: For an early seminoma, options after surgery include surveillance, a single course of the chemotherapy drug carboplatin, or radiotherapy, although radiotherapy is now mainly kept for people who cannot have chemotherapy.
note: Search summary of CUH stage I seminoma, Macmillan and CRUK pages; the earlier 'sometimes needs radiotherapy' framing overstated radiotherapy.

sentence: For an early non-seminoma, surveillance, meaning regular check-ups and tests, is an option when the risk of the cancer returning is low, and the alternative is usually a short course of chemotherapy.
note: Search summary of CRUK/CUH: surveillance when relapse risk low, otherwise usually one cycle of BEP chemotherapy (or lymph node surgery).

sentence: Which option is suggested depends on the type of tumour, the stage and the chance of the cancer coming back.
note: Search summary: risk-stratified decisions by type and stage. Original 'specialist team explains' removed as unretrieved.

sentence: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy may affect sperm production, and Cancer Research UK says fertility can often return after treatment, though this may take time.
note: CRUK/Orchid fertility pages. Lymph node surgery not retrieved, removed.

sentence: In some cases sperm production does not fully recover, although the National Cancer Institute says most men can father children after treatment.
note: Search summary: in some cases sperm production may not fully recover; NCI: most men can father children after treatment.

sentence: Orchid says sperm banking may be advised before an orchidectomy if chemotherapy is likely to be needed or the other testicle may produce little sperm.
note: Orchid fertility page. Earlier 'before any treatment other than removal' contradicted by this.

sentence: Macmillan says that a person who has not stored sperm can still do so after surgery if further treatment is offered.
note: Macmillan surgery page via search summary.

sentence: Orchid notes that banking has limits, as a low sperm count, poor sperm quality and the freezing and thawing process can all affect the sperm, and that stored sperm is held for 10 years at first, with the period able to be extended.
note: Orchid fertility page.

sentence: Orchid and Macmillan both provide information on fertility and sex after testicular cancer.
note: Orchid fertility page; Macmillan sex-and-fertility page.

sentence: Studies report that testosterone levels can fall after treatment in some people, and reviews recommend checking testosterone levels during follow-up.
note: PMC5384966, PMC5987955 and related reviews; prevalence varies with treatment.

sentence: Testicular cancer is generally described as highly treatable, and MedlinePlus calls it one of the most treatable and curable cancers.
note: MedlinePlus.
